title: Within one pair of arcs, must the two radii be equal?
description: A question from the book asks whether the arc from X and the arc from Y in one pair may have different radii. An arc of one radius from X and an arc of another radius from Y are drawn, and a congruent triangle pair shows that their meeting point is not on the perpendicular bisector.
teaching_notes: One idea: every point of the perpendicular bisector is equally far from X and Y, so a meeting point at unequal distances is not on it. Watch for students who think any two arcs that meet give a usable point.

video_script.why: The child has seen that the pairs of arcs may differ from each other, and has not yet asked whether the two arcs inside one pair may differ.
video_script.substitution: The construction is done in the same way as the example in the book, with the arc from Y given a different radius, and then one pair of congruent triangles shows what goes wrong.
video_script.anchor: In one pair of arcs, must the arc from X and the arc from Y have the same radius?
video_script.payoff_line: Yes, within one pair the two radii must be equal

final_answer.value: Yes. Within one pair the two arcs must have the same radius; otherwise the meeting point is not equally far from X and Y, and every point of the perpendicular bisector is (SAS), so it would not lie on the perpendicular bisector
final_answer.spoken: yes, within one pair the two radii must be equal, otherwise the meeting point is not on the perpendicular bisector

never_show: the answer yes before the answer line
maths_rules: An arc of radius r from X and an arc of radius s from Y, with s not equal to r, meet at P: PX = r and PY = s, so PX is not equal to PY.
Let Q be any point of the perpendicular bisector, and let QO meet XY at O. Triangle QOX is congruent to triangle QOY by SAS (OX = OY, angle QOX = angle QOY = 90 degrees, QO common), so QX = QY.
Every point of the perpendicular bisector is equally far from X and Y. P is not, so P is not on the perpendicular bisector.
video_script.design: One idea: a point on the perpendicular bisector must be equally far from X and Y, so the two arcs of one pair need one radius. The construction of the book's example is repeated with a changed radius for Y.
